reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham
bases: A wire report said a party was pursuing Cunningham after an alleged attack on a white youth and that there was 'much talk of lynching him' (A1), but he was arrested by officers and no mob action against him is reported (A2); it is at most a threatened lynching.

No one was killed by a mob: the accused was arrested and taken by officers toward the Court House (A2), and the only sign of mob intent is the wire's 'much talk of lynching' (A1); the pretext would have been the alleged attack on Byers.

The talk of lynching and the pursuing party appear in one Columbia wire reprinted verbatim (A1, A3, A4); the attack and the arrest are confirmed independently by state papers (A2, A6), which also contradict the wire's report that Byers died.

summary.text: The threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham occurred in late May 1888 near Wilkinsville, in Union County, South Carolina, when a party pursued Cunningham, a Black tenant accused of striking a white youth, Gunning Byers, on the head, amid what a wire report called 'much talk of lynching him.'
Cunningham was arrested by officers the next day and taken toward the courthouse, and no violence against him was reported.
The case drew notice chiefly through a Columbia dispatch that reported Byers murdered, a claim local papers later contradicted.
Cunningham was a tenant of William Byers, described as one of the largest planters in that part of the county.
According to the Greenville News, the two had a 'difficulty' a few days before, after which Cunningham swore vengeance against the whole Byers family.
Cunningham was accused of attacking Byers's son Gunning, about 16, on a Thursday or Friday evening, about May 24 or 25, and then fleeing.

A Columbia dispatch of May 27 said he met the youth alone in the woods and dealt him 'a mortal blow on the head with an ax', that a party was already in pursuit, and that unless Cunningham reached the authorities first he would 'doubtless never come to trial.'

A Spartanburg dispatch dated Sunday reported instead that Cunningham had been arrested at noon the day before, hiding out several miles from home, and that officers had started toward the Court House with him.

Byers survived, according to a Union County correspondent of the Yorkville Enquirer, who wrote that a neighboring physician, Dr. M. J. Walker, removed twenty-four pieces of fractured skull and that the patient was 'doing well.'
The correspondent withheld details because the matter 'will undergo a legal investigation', but no report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.
The Atlanta Constitution printed the Columbia special under the headlines 'Swift Vengeance Taken' and 'A South Carolina Desperado's Terrible Crime', calling the attack a 'brutal murder.'
The same text ran unchanged in the Anderson Intelligencer on May 31 and the Charlotte Messenger on June 2, after the arrest had already been reported in South Carolina.
The Savannah Morning News also reported the youth killed, naming him William Byers.

The Yorkville Enquirer took a different course, reprinting the arrest and Byers's improving condition and then a correspondent who called the published statements 'quite erroneous—particularly that of the Atlanta Constitution.'
Accounts differ on the weapon: the wire and the Greenville News said an ax, while the Union County correspondent described a stone of about four pounds thrown some twenty-eight yards.
The correspondent also called the accused 'Jerry Cunningham' and placed the attack on the Byers plantation rather than in the woods.

accounts.label: Columbia wire
accounts.gist: Cunningham killed Byers with an ax in the woods to avenge a dispute with his father; a party was in pursuit and there was 'much talk of lynching him'.

accounts.label: Greenville News and Spartanburg dispatch (via Yorkville Enquirer)
accounts.gist: Cunningham struck Byers with an axe, inflicting a wound expected to prove fatal; Byers was later resting and rational, and Cunningham was arrested and taken by officers toward the Court House.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News paragraph
accounts.gist: Cunningham hit 'young William Byers' in the head with an ax, killing him.

accounts.label: Union County correspondent ('Sigma')
accounts.gist: Byers was wounded, not killed, by a stone of about four pounds thrown some 28 yards; he walked home, was treated, and was doing well; earlier accounts were erroneous.

framing.detail: The wire headed the story 'Swift Vengeance Taken' and 'A South Carolina Desperado's Terrible Crime', called it a 'brutal murder', and treated a lynching as likely without criticism.
The Anderson Intelligencer and the Charlotte Messenger ran the wire text unchanged, the Messenger keeping the 'Swift Vengeance Taken' headline.
The Yorkville Enquirer reported the arrest and Byers's condition and printed a local correspondent who rebuked the published accounts as 'quite erroneous'.

versions.value: wound expected to prove fatal, then resting quietly and rational

conflicts.note: The local correspondent, writing latest and from the neighborhood with details of the treatment, is the better evidence; he names the Atlanta Constitution's account as erroneous.

versions.value: a stone of about four pounds thrown some 28 yards

conflicts.note: Only the local correspondent describes seeing the stone.
